title: Gradients, constrained optimisation and safeguards
objectives: Distinguish feasible global/local/stationary points and derive the convex first-order constrained condition, including a boundary optimum with nonzero gradient.
Derive and trace a bounded Armijo backtracking step for a stated quadratic, preserving the iterate on search failure and distinguishing acceptance/stationarity from a general optimum certificate.
Apply gradients, constrained optimisation and safeguards invariants safely and identify scope boundaries.
motivation: An optimization problem specifies an objective f to minimize, a domain and a feasible set C. A feasible point belongs to C; a global minimizer has f(x*)≤f(y) for every feasible y.

blocks.md: An optimization problem specifies an objective f to minimize, a domain and a feasible set C. A feasible point belongs to C; a global minimizer has f(x*)≤f(y) for every feasible y. A local minimizer needs this only for feasible y in a neighborhood. A stationary differentiable interior point has ∇f=0, but without convexity it may be a minimum, maximum or saddle. A solver exit status is not a substitute for feasibility, derivative correctness, objective meaning or a global-optimality argument.

For differentiable f, the first-order change along d is ∇f(x)ᵀd. A direction with negative directional derivative is locally descending for sufficiently small positive steps that stay in the domain. In the chosen Euclidean coordinate geometry, d=-∇f gives slope -||∇f||² when the gradient is nonzero. It need not remain feasible under constraints. Coordinates with different units require an explicit scaling/metric; a bare learning rate is not invariant to changing the units of one coordinate.

A convex feasible set contains every segment between its points; a differentiable convex f lies above each tangent plane: f(y)≥f(x)+∇f(x)ᵀ(y-x). For x∈C, the condition ∇f(x)ᵀ(y-x)≥0 for ALL y∈C therefore proves global optimality. Conversely, if the condition fails for a feasible y, convexity of C keeps x+t(y-x) feasible and the negative derivative decreases f for small positive t, contradicting optimality. This gives a necessary/sufficient condition for differentiable convex optimization, not a blanket certificate for arbitrary nonlinear constraints/objectives.

blocks.title: A constrained optimum need not have zero gradient
items: Minimize f(x)=(x-3)² over 0≤x≤1. Its unconstrained minimizer 3 is infeasible. On this interval f'(x)=2(x-3)<0, so increasing x decreases f.
The constrained solution is x*=1, with objective 4 and derivative -4. For every feasible y≤1, (-4)(y-1)≥0. The convex first-order condition holds despite nonzero derivative.

For a general target t on a nonempty interval [l,u], minimizing (x-t)² gives min(u,max(l,t)). If t is inside, it gives zero loss; if t>u, every feasible point is farther from t than u, and similarly at l when t<l.
A singleton feasible interval has only one possible point, whatever the derivative. This is a feasibility fact, not evidence that the unconstrained gradient vanished.

blocks.caption: Expected lines: 1 4 -4; 0 4 4; 1/2 0 0; then 1. This helper solves ONLY one exact squared-distance objective on one closed interval. Clipping a general unconstrained optimizer is not a valid general constrained-optimization method.

blocks.md:
Without convexity, f'(0)=0 for f(x)=-x² but 0 is a maximum; f(x)=x³ has a stationary non-extremum at 0. In two variables x²-y² has a saddle at (0,0). Convexity can make a stationary point globally optimal; strict convexity gives at most one minimizer but does not by itself ensure one is attained on an open or unbounded domain. Nonempty constraints and a stopping tolerance alone do not establish existence.

A descent direction does not justify any step length. For f=(x-3)² at x=0, gradient=-6 and d=6. Step t=1 gives x+=6 and objective 9, unchanged from 9; t=2 gives x+=12 and objective 81, worse. Step t=1/2 gives x+=3 and objective 0. Step-size choice matters even on a one-dimensional convex quadratic.

Armijo sufficient decrease requires f(x+t*d)≤f(x)+c*t*∇f(x)ᵀd, with 0<c<1 and positive t. Because the directional slope is negative, the right-hand side is below f(x). Differentiability gives f(x+t*d)=f(x)+t*slope+o(t); subtracting the Armijo right side leaves (1-c)*t*slope+o(t), negative for sufficiently small positive t provided the domain allows those steps. Backtracking shrinks t by β∈(0,1) until this check holds. This local existence argument assumes a true descent derivative and an evaluable smooth neighborhood; it is not an iteration-count or global-convergence guarantee.

blocks.caption: Expected lines: accepted 3 1/2 1; stationary 3 0 0; line-search-limit 0 0 1. The fixed exact quadratic uses c=1/4, beta=1/2. At t=1 the Armijo RHS is 0 while the candidate objective is 9, so the first trial fails; t=1/2 has RHS 4.5 and objective 0, so it succeeds. A one-attempt budget cannot reach the accepted step and returns the original iterate, not a fake optimum.

blocks.md: The helper computes a SINGLE unconstrained step on one fixed exact rational polynomial. It does not run a general optimizer, implement projected Armijo, KKT multipliers or certify production risk allocation. A floating general implementation also needs finite objective/gradient checks, representable positive steps, domain/feasibility checks, evaluation/iteration budgets, tolerance/scaling policy and explicit search/gradient failure states. Projection changes the path and acceptance logic; do not reuse the unprojected slope formula blindly after clipping.

Record why a run stopped: small gradient under its chosen geometry, feasible projected-gradient/KKT residual when applicable, small step, objective-change tolerance, evaluation cap or failed line search. A tiny step can mean rounding or a bad direction; a small objective change can mean poor scaling. Assess feasibility and residuals against tolerances, compare analytic/small reference cases, and separate numerical stationarity from model validation and out-of-sample utility. No method here authorizes a live allocation or transaction.

Independent transfer: derive the interval optimum for target -2 on [0,1], verify the feasible-direction condition and compare with target 3. Trace the fixed quadratic step with initial t=2 and predict rejected trials before code. Construct a stationary maximum and explain why a gradient norm check would miss the distinction. Specify what an iteration/evaluation cap should report without mislabeling an unfinished run converged.

References: [Boyd/Vandenberghe convexity and feasible first-order criterion, sections 3.1.3 and 4.2.3](https://stanford.edu/~boyd/cvxbook/bv_cvxbook.pdf), [CMU gradient descent/backtracking](https://www.stat.cmu.edu/~ryantibs/convexopt-F16/lectures/grad-descent.pdf), and [Stanford descent methods](https://web.stanford.edu/class/ee364a/lectures/unconstrained.pdf). Own fixed-quadratic code is standard-library only and makes no general numerical optimizer/runtime claim.

guidedExercise.prompt: A solver stops after tiny objective changes. What evidence would you require before calling the result optimal?
hints: Checks feasible residuals under explicit assumptions.
Avoids a model or action guarantee from status alone.
guidedExercise.solution: Check the stop status/budget, feasibility, derivative correctness and scaling, an appropriate gradient/projected/KKT residual, convexity/global-optimality conditions or bounded claims, and reference cases. Separate numerical solution from model validity and action authority.

independentExercise.prompt: Write a small test case that deliberately breaks the contract boundary in "Gradients, constrained optimisation and safeguards" and verify how your implementation rejects or handles it.
hints: Test zero, negative, empty, duplicate, and boundary values.
Confirm both time/memory complexity and numerical precision remain within spec.

commonMistakes: The convex feasible-direction condition is the appropriate test, not an unconstrained zero-gradient rule. (Every feasible displacement from 1 is nonpositive, giving nonnegative gradient dot displacement.)
For example -x² has zero derivative at its maximum 0. (A maximum or saddle can also be stationary.)
Acceptance checks a particular objective decrease under a stated rule, not a full optimization or modeling certificate. (The negative slope makes the Armijo RHS lower than the old objective.)
realWorldApplication: Used directly across production quantitative research, execution systems, and validation pipelines.
quantFinanceApplication: Applies rigorous engineering contracts to quantitative modeling and live trading infrastructure.
summary: Feasibility and the objective define optimality.

Convex first-order conditions explain boundary solutions with nonzero gradients; safeguarded step acceptance, stationary status and search-budget failure are distinct from general convergence or model validity.

quiz.prompt: For minimizing (x-3)² over [0,1], which statement is correct?
options: x=1 is optimal even though f'(1)=-4
No optimum exists unless the gradient is 0
Every feasible point is equally good
quiz.explanation: The convex feasible-direction condition is the appropriate test, not an unconstrained zero-gradient rule. (Every feasible displacement from 1 is nonpositive, giving nonnegative gradient dot displacement.)

quiz.prompt: What does ∇f(x)=0 alone prove for a differentiable nonconvex interior problem?
options: A feasible boundary optimum with known multipliers
Only stationarity, not a global minimum
quiz.explanation: For example -x² has zero derivative at its maximum 0. (A maximum or saddle can also be stationary.)

quiz.prompt: With a true negative directional slope, what does Armijo acceptance establish at that trial?
options: A stated sufficient decrease for that objective/step
Global optimality for every nonconvex problem
The gradient implementation is mathematically correct
quiz.explanation: Acceptance checks a particular objective decrease under a stated rule, not a full optimization or modeling certificate. (The negative slope makes the Armijo RHS lower than the old objective.)

quiz.prompt: If the permitted line-search trials are exhausted, what should this helper do?
options: Return the best-looking point as a certified optimum
Silently increase the trial budget forever
Keep the original iterate and report line-search-limit
Hide the failure by returning stationary
quiz.explanation: A bounded search needs an honest status and an unchanged iterate on failure in this helper contract. (The failure is explicit and the failed candidate is not committed.)

quiz.prompt: For min (x-3)² on [0,1], what is the objective at the constrained optimum?
quiz.explanation: The optimum is x=1, so (1-3)²=4. The unconstrained objective 0 is unattainable in the feasible set.
